title: Conditional UI Patterns
learning_outcomes: Explain how Conditional UI Patterns relates to Rendering, Lists, and Conditional UI.
Apply Showing and hiding elements in a small React or JavaScript example and describe the expected result.
Test one edge/failure case and identify a maintainable, accessible fix.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study Conditional UI Patterns as part of Rendering, Lists, and Conditional UI. The syllabus topics are kept below, then connected to a small example you can inspect and adapt.
content.why_it_matters: Showing and hiding elements determines how changing information drives the UI. Update through the state setter with immutable replacements; use a functional updater when the next value depends on the previous one.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Showing and hiding elements determines how changing information drives the UI. Update through the state setter with immutable replacements; use a functional updater when the next value depends on the previous one. Start with one responsibility at a time: identify the data, describe the expected interface, then decide which event, state update, request, or runtime boundary changes the result.

content_blocks.code:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

return <button onClick={() => setCount(value => value + 1)}>Count: {count}</button>;
content_blocks.expected_output: Each click queues an update based on the previous state, and React updates the rendered count.

Server rendering and framework APIs require their stated runtime.

content_blocks.title: Version and environment note
content_blocks.text: This course assumes the React 19.3 documentation snapshot dated 2026-10-12. Core component, JSX, props, state, and event concepts apply broadly; modern APIs and server rendering must be checked against the stated React version and the framework/runtime in use.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating Conditional UI Patterns. Include the relevant subtopic “Showing and hiding elements”, explain the expected UI/result, and verify one normal case plus one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named concept rather than merely mentioning it.
The expected visible or logged result is documented and reproducible.
At least one boundary, empty, loading, or failure case is handled or explained.
The implementation remains accessible and does not introduce avoidable mutation, stale state, or insecure client-only trust.
hints: Start with the smallest part of “Showing and hiding elements” that can be observed independently.
Write down what should appear before changing the code; then change one input at a time.
Use the browser console, React Developer Tools, or the appropriate test/runtime to isolate a mismatch.
content.expected_output: Each click queues an update based on the previous state, and React updates the rendered count.

common_mistakes.problem: The example handles only the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real UI receives empty values, delayed responses, and invalid input.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one explicit edge/failure case and document the expected message or state.

common_mistakes.problem: The example stores redundant data or mutates an existing array/object.
common_mistakes.why: The displayed result can drift from the source data or React may not observe the intended change.
common_mistakes.fix: Derive values where possible and create a new value when updating state.

common_mistakes.problem: A browser or framework capability is assumed to exist everywhere.
common_mistakes.why: Availability can depend on the host runtime, React version, and framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the official reference, declare the runtime/version, and provide a fallback when appropriate.
